representation: stepwise educational schematic; no pharmacokinetic or physiologic simulation
medical_boundary: Mechanism and receptor engagement do not establish human therapeutic benefit, dosing, clinical safety or restored homeostasis. Not medical advice.

sources.note: Anandamide has alternative synthesis and degradation pathways; metabolic diagrams are simplified.

journeys.name: 2-AG at a neural synapse
journeys.subtitle: A documented example of retrograde signaling
journeys.model: Cellular and neuronal circuit experiments, reviewed in synaptic physiology literature.
journeys.summary: A locally produced endocannabinoid can travel backward across a synapse, adjust presynaptic signaling and then be degraded.
journeys.boundary: This schematic describes one studied mechanism, not every neuron, a real-time simulation, human cognition improvement, or a cannabis treatment outcome.

steps.title: Activity at a synapse
steps.description: In some neuronal circuits, postsynaptic activity triggers local signaling that can mobilize endocannabinoid production.
steps.context_note: The initiating signals and contributing pathways differ among synapses.

steps.title: DAGL contributes to 2-AG synthesis
steps.description: Diacylglycerol lipase helps convert diacylglycerol precursors into 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG).
steps.context_note: This is a simplified enzyme route, not the only route regulating 2-AG.

steps.title: 2-AG engages presynaptic CB1
steps.description: 2-AG can signal across the synaptic cleft toward CB1 receptors on a presynaptic terminal.
steps.context_note: This specific retrograde organization is documented in selected synapses.

steps.title: Neurotransmitter release can be reduced
steps.description: Presynaptic CB1 activation can modulate calcium-channel activity and suppress transmitter release in relevant experimental circuits.
steps.context_note: Direction and significance depend on circuit context; less transmission is not automatically healthier.

steps.title: MAGL helps end the signal
steps.description: Monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL) is a major enzyme involved in the breakdown of 2-AG.
steps.context_note: Other metabolic processes also participate; this is not a quantitative timeline.

journeys.name: Anandamide: formation and breakdown
journeys.subtitle: An endogenous lipid with multiple metabolic routes
journeys.model: Biochemical, cellular and animal pathway studies summarized in review literature.
journeys.summary: Anandamide (AEA) is produced from endogenous precursors and broken down through enzyme-regulated routes; simplified diagrams are not the full biochemistry.
journeys.boundary: The existence of anandamide pathways does not diagnose an 'ECS deficiency', establish an individualized target, or show that consuming cannabis improves health.

steps.title: One AEA production route uses NAPE-PLD
steps.description: NAPE-PLD participates in the biosynthesis of anandamide (AEA) from membrane-derived N-acylphosphatidylethanolamine precursors.
steps.context_note: Alternative synthesis routes exist; this is not a unique enzyme for all AEA formation.

steps.title: AEA acts as an endogenous messenger
steps.description: Anandamide belongs to the body's endocannabinoid signaling system; its local actions depend on receptor, cell and physiological context.
steps.context_note: AEA is not a plant phytocannabinoid; its downstream actions are not uniform throughout the body.

steps.title: FAAH contributes to AEA hydrolysis
steps.description: Fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) is a major enzyme that breaks down anandamide and participates in signal termination.
steps.context_note: FAAH is important but not the only degradative enzyme or route.

steps.title: Redundant pathways prevent a one-switch story
steps.description: Alternative synthesis and degradation routes mean that a single arrow or enzyme label cannot explain every AEA response.
steps.context_note: The atlas is an explanatory diagram, not a control panel for manipulating a patient's biochemistry.

journeys.name: CB2 in immune-cell contexts
journeys.subtitle: A receptor pathway, not an immune-boosting promise
journeys.model: Immune-cell receptor characterization and mainly preclinical inflammatory signaling studies.
journeys.summary: CB2-linked signaling is researched in immune cells, where receptor expression and downstream effects can change with cell type and activation.
journeys.boundary: A CB2 pathway is not proof that cannabis boosts immunity, cures inflammation or treats autoimmune disease in people.

steps.title: Immune cell identity matters
steps.description: CB2 receptors are prominently associated with immune-cell populations; expression depends on the cell type and its activation state.
steps.context_note: The same CB2 distribution is not assumed for every cell, organ or person.

steps.title: Receptor-linked signaling is investigated
steps.description: Researchers examine how CB2-linked G-protein signaling affects immune-cell responses in specific experimental systems.
steps.context_note: Results may vary by experimental agonist, species, tissue and inflammatory condition.

steps.title: Inflammatory mediator pathways may change
steps.description: In selected cell and animal models, CB2-related signaling can modulate immune mediators and neuroimmune processes.
steps.context_note: An immune signaling change is not inherently beneficial and cannot establish human clinical effectiveness.

steps.title: A pathway is not a patient outcome
steps.description: The mechanistic result must not be promoted into evidence that a cannabis product treats human inflammatory or autoimmune disease.
steps.context_note: Controlled human trials for a specified intervention and condition are needed to assess efficacy and safety.
